teaching.h: Hebrew reads right to left — the very first adjustment
teaching.p: This is the single biggest habit shift for a new learner: Hebrew text flows right to left, and numbers within it still read left to right. Everything else follows from getting used to this direction.
teaching.exTranslation: shalom — hello/peace

teaching.h: No lowercase, and five letters change shape at the end of a word
teaching.p: Unlike Latin scripts, Hebrew has one letter form — no capital/lowercase distinction. But five letters (כ, מ, נ, פ, צ) take a special 'final form' when they're the last letter of a word.
teaching.exTranslation: melekh — king (note the final ך)

teaching.h: Vowels are usually invisible in everyday writing
teaching.p: Modern Hebrew is normally written WITHOUT vowel marks (nikkud) — native readers infer the vowels from context and familiarity with the word. Learning materials (including this course) show nikkud to help you, but real-world signs and books usually won't.
teaching.exTranslation: sefer — book (vowels not shown, but pronounced 'SEH-fer')

teaching.h: A few sounds that don't exist in English
teaching.p: ח and ר are the two most distinctive: ח is a raspy back-of-throat sound (similar to the 'ch' in Bach), and ר is a guttural r, not the tongue-tap r of Spanish or the retroflex r of English.
teaching.exTranslation: chaver — friend

teaching.h: Every noun is masculine or feminine — no neuter
teaching.p: Simpler than German or Russian in one way: Hebrew only has two genders, not three. But like those languages, gender affects verbs and adjectives that go with the noun.
teaching.exTranslation: sefer (book, m), delet (door, f)

teaching.h: The ending ה often signals feminine
teaching.p: Not a perfect rule, but a strong pattern — many feminine nouns end in ה (ah sound).
teaching.exTranslation: morah — female teacher

teaching.h: Plurals: ים for masculine, ות for feminine (usually)
teaching.p: Like the gender ending rule, this is a strong pattern with real exceptions you'll pick up over time.
teaching.exTranslation: sfarim (books), morot (female teachers)

teaching.h: No indefinite article at all
teaching.p: Hebrew has no word for 'a/an' — you simply say the noun by itself, and context tells you it's indefinite.
teaching.exTranslation: sefer — a book (no article needed)

quiz.q: How many genders does Hebrew have?
Which ending often signals a feminine noun?
The masculine plural ending is usually:
Does Hebrew have a word for 'a/an'?

teaching.h: One tiny letter attached directly to the word
teaching.p: Unlike English's separate word 'the', Hebrew's definite article is just the letter ה attached to the FRONT of the noun — no space, no separate word.
teaching.exTranslation: sefer (a book) → ha-sefer (the book)

teaching.h: It attaches to adjectives too, when describing a definite noun
teaching.p: If the noun is definite, any adjective describing it also gets its own ה — both words carry the article.
teaching.exTranslation: ha-sefer ha-gadol — the big book

teaching.h: Some letters trigger a small pronunciation shift
teaching.p: When ה attaches to a word starting with certain letters, the vowel sound underneath it changes slightly — this is a pronunciation detail that becomes automatic with listening practice, not something to memorize as a rule upfront.

quiz.q: ___ספר (the book — add the definite article letter)

options: a letter attached to the noun
quiz.answer: a letter attached to the noun

quiz.q: When a noun is definite, its adjective:

options: to the front of the word
to the end of the word
quiz.answer: to the front of the word

teaching.h: Present tense is genuinely simpler than you'd expect
teaching.p: Hebrew present tense isn't conjugated the way past/future are — instead, it uses a special verb FORM (called a participle/beinoni) that changes based on gender and number, not person. This is a real structural difference from European languages.
teaching.exTranslation: ani kotev (I write, masculine speaker), at kotevet (you write, feminine)

teaching.h: The pronoun set
teaching.p: אני (I), אתה (you, m), את (you, f), הוא (he), היא (she), אנחנו (we), אתם (you all, m), אתן (you all, f), הם (they, m), הן (they, f).
teaching.exTranslation: I, you (m), you (f), he, she

teaching.h: The present-tense verb changes with the SUBJECT's gender, not 'person'
teaching.p: Notice above: 'kotev' vs 'kotevet' isn't about who's speaking, it's about whether the subject is male or female — a genuinely different logic from French/Spanish/German verb conjugation.
teaching.exTranslation: hu kotev (he writes), hi kotevet (she writes)

quiz.q: Hebrew present tense changes based on:
options: gender and number of the subject
quiz.answer: gender and number of the subject

quiz.q: The Hebrew present-tense verb form is called:

teaching.h: Past tense DOES conjugate by person
teaching.p: Unlike present tense, past tense verbs change endings for I/you/he/she/we/they — much closer to what a European-language learner would expect.
teaching.exTranslation: ani katavti (I wrote), atah katavta (you wrote, m)

teaching.h: The root system underlies everything
teaching.p: Most Hebrew verbs are built from a three-letter root that carries the core meaning, with different vowel patterns and prefixes/suffixes layered on for tense and person. כ-ת-ב (k-t-v) is the 'writing' root running through every form you've seen so far.
teaching.exTranslation: katavti (I wrote), kotev (writing, present), ekhtov (I will write) — same root, different forms

teaching.h: Full past-tense pattern for one verb
teaching.ex: כתבתי, כתבת, כתבת, כתב, כתבה, כתבנו, כתבתם, כתבו
teaching.exTranslation: I wrote, you wrote (m), you wrote (f), he wrote, she wrote, we wrote, you all wrote, they wrote

quiz.q: Does past tense conjugate by person (I/you/he)?
Most Hebrew verbs are built from a root of how many letters?

teaching.h: The basic categories, working similarly to what you'd expect
teaching.p: שם עצם (noun), פועל (verb), שם תואר (adjective), תואר הפועל (adverb) — the categories themselves are familiar even though the words and the writing system are new.
teaching.exTranslation: runs, quickly, teacher

teaching.h: Adjectives come AFTER the noun, and must agree with it
teaching.p: This is the reverse of English order, and the adjective's gender/number must match the noun exactly — same agreement logic as Spanish or German, just positioned differently.
teaching.exTranslation: sefer gadol — a big book (literally: book big)

teaching.h: Prepositions often attach directly to the following word
teaching.p: Small prepositions like ב (in/at), ל (to/for), and מ (from) are typically prefixed directly onto the next word, not written as separate words — similar in spirit to the definite article ה.
teaching.exTranslation: ba-bayit — in the house (ב + הבית, contracted)

options: big book (word for word in English order)

quiz.q: Small prepositions like ב (in) are usually:
options: prefixed directly onto the next word
quiz.answer: prefixed directly onto the next word

quiz.q: Adjectives must agree with their noun in:

teaching.h: Basic word order: Subject-Verb-Object, like English
teaching.p: This is genuinely reassuring for an English speaker — the underlying logical order matches, even though the script and direction are totally different.
teaching.exTranslation: David okhel tapuach — David eats an apple

teaching.h: No verb 'to be' needed in the present tense
teaching.p: Just like Russian, Hebrew present-tense sentences typically OMIT any equivalent of 'is/are' — you just place the two things next to each other.
teaching.exTranslation: David moreh — David is a teacher (literally: David teacher)

teaching.h: Yes/no questions often just use intonation or האם
teaching.p: You can turn a statement into a question just by rising intonation (in speech) or by adding האם at the front (more formal/written).
teaching.exTranslation: ha-im David moreh? — Is David a teacher?

quiz.q: Does Hebrew present tense need a 'to be' verb?
___ דוד מורה? (is David a teacher — question marker)
One way to ask a yes/no question is:
options: always moving the verb to the front

teaching.h: Hebrew's own way of showing possession
teaching.p: Instead of an apostrophe-s or a separate 'of', Hebrew often shows 'X of Y' by putting two nouns next to each other and slightly changing the FIRST one's form — this pairing is called smichut.
teaching.exTranslation: beit sefer — school (literally: house-of book)

teaching.h: The first noun often shortens or changes
teaching.p: בית (bayit, house) becomes בית (beit) in construct form — a subtle vowel shift that's worth listening for rather than memorizing as a spelling rule.
teaching.exTranslation: house + book = school

teaching.h: Only the second noun can take the definite article
teaching.p: In a smichut pair, ה attaches to the SECOND word only, and that makes the whole phrase definite.
teaching.exTranslation: beit ha-sefer — the school

quiz.q: Smichut is Hebrew's way of expressing:
In a smichut pair, the definite article ה attaches to:

teaching.h: Future tense conjugates by person, using prefixes
teaching.p: Unlike present tense (which changes by gender/number) and similar to past tense (which conjugates fully), future tense adds a PREFIX to the root that identifies the subject.
teaching.exTranslation: ani ekhtov (I will write), atah tikhtov (you will write, m)

teaching.h: Full future-tense pattern
teaching.ex: אכתוב, תכתוב, תכתבי, יכתוב, תכתוב, נכתוב, תכתבו, יכתבו
teaching.exTranslation: I will write, you (m) will write, you (f) will write, he will write, she will write, we will write, you all will write, they will write

teaching.h: The future tense also works as a command form
teaching.p: In casual Hebrew, the future-tense 'you' form is often used to give instructions or requests, especially in the negative — a genuinely practical thing to recognize when someone's asking you (not) to do something.
teaching.exTranslation: al tid'ag — don't worry

quiz.q: The future-tense form is sometimes used for:

teaching.h: Real conditions with אם
teaching.p: אם (if) plus normal tense — for realistic situations, similar to how German/Spanish handle it.
teaching.ex: אם ירד גשם, אני אשאר בבית
teaching.exTranslation: im yered geshem, ani eshaer ba-bayit — If it rains, I'll stay home

teaching.h: Hypothetical conditions with אילו
teaching.p: For unreal or unlikely situations, אילו replaces אם and pairs with the היה (was) form for a 'would have been' feel.
teaching.exTranslation: ilu hayiti ashir, hayiti nosea — If I were rich, I would travel

teaching.h: היה shows up constantly in hypotheticals
teaching.p: This is Hebrew's rough equivalent of 'would' — it appears in both halves of a hypothetical sentence.
teaching.exTranslation: hayiti (I would/was), hayita (you would/were, m)

quiz.q: ___ ירד גשם, אני אשאר בבית (if — realistic)
היה is roughly Hebrew's equivalent of:

teaching.h: A clause needs a subject and verb — same test as any language
teaching.p: This universal grammatical test still applies in Hebrew, even with the unfamiliar script.
teaching.exTranslation: hi ratzah, ki hi ich'ra — she ran, because she was late

teaching.h: כי and מפני ש both mean 'because'
teaching.p: כי is shorter and more common in everyday speech; מפני ש is a bit more formal.
teaching.exTranslation: she ran because she was late

teaching.h: ש attaches directly to introduce a clause, like English 'that'
teaching.p: Similar to how ה attaches for 'the', ש attaches to the front of a word to introduce a subordinate clause.
teaching.exTranslation: ani yode'a she-atah ayef — I know that you are tired

options: attaches to the front of the next word
stands alone as a separate word
quiz.answer: attaches to the front of the next word

quiz.q: מפני ש compared to כי is:

teaching.h: Binyanim — Hebrew's unique verb-pattern system
teaching.p: This doesn't map neatly onto European grammar: Hebrew verbs fall into 7 patterns (binyanim) built from the same 3-letter root, and switching between certain patterns is how Hebrew expresses active vs. passive, among other things.
teaching.exTranslation: katav (he wrote, active), nikhtav (it was written, passive)

teaching.h: Same root, different pattern, related meaning
teaching.p: This is the elegant part once it clicks: כ-ת-ב (root: write) appears in both, just wrapped in a different binyan pattern to shift the meaning.
teaching.exTranslation: ha-sefer nikhtav — the book was written

teaching.h: You don't need all 7 binyanim to start speaking
teaching.p: This is genuinely a longer-term learning project — for now, just recognize that when a verb 'looks different but related' to one you know, it's likely the same root in a different binyan.

options: verb patterns built from a shared root
quiz.answer: verb patterns built from a shared root

quiz.q: How many binyanim does Hebrew have?

teaching.h: Direct speech — the exact words
teaching.exTranslation: hi amrah: "ani ayefah" — She said: "I am tired"

teaching.h: Indirect speech with ש
teaching.p: Same ש you saw in Lesson 11, now introducing reported speech instead of just any subordinate clause.
teaching.exTranslation: hi amrah she-hi ayefah — She said that she was tired

teaching.h: Tense mostly stays the same when reporting
teaching.p: Similar to Russian and Mandarin, Hebrew doesn't require the elaborate tense-backshift that English does — the original tense usually just carries over.

quiz.q: Does Hebrew require extensive tense-backshift like English?

options: She said that she was tired
quiz.answer: She said that she was tired

teaching.h: No capital letters, same as Mandarin/Arabic
teaching.p: Hebrew has one letter form throughout, so none of the capitalization rules from European languages apply here.

teaching.h: Punctuation marks generally match English usage
teaching.p: Periods, commas, question marks work basically the same way as in English — the visual direction just flips because the text itself flows right to left.
teaching.exTranslation: mah shlomkha? — How are you?

teaching.h: Numbers are written left to right, even inside RTL text
teaching.p: This creates a genuinely interesting visual effect: within a right-to-left sentence, any numerals still read in their normal left-to-right order.
teaching.exTranslation: yesh li 25 sfarim — I have 25 books

teaching.h: Nikkud (vowel points) appear mainly in children's books, poetry, and prayer texts
teaching.p: Outside of learning materials, expect to encounter unvocalized Hebrew almost everywhere — this course shows nikkud specifically to help you learn, but real fluency means getting comfortable reading without it.

teaching.h: Prepositions with attached pronoun suffixes
teaching.p: Instead of a separate word for 'to me/to you/to him', Hebrew often attaches a pronoun SUFFIX directly onto the preposition — a compact structure with no real English equivalent.
teaching.exTranslation: li (to me), lekha (to you, m), lo (to him)

teaching.h: The infinitive form (שם הפועל)
teaching.p: Formed with a ל- prefix on the root, similar in function to English 'to + verb'.
teaching.exTranslation: likhtov — to write

teaching.h: Construct chains can go three nouns deep
teaching.p: The smichut structure from Lesson 8 can extend further — 'the door of the house of the teacher' style chains, though this gets genuinely complex and is more of an awareness point than something to actively produce yet.
teaching.exTranslation: delet beit ha-sefer — the door of the school

quiz.q: The infinitive prefix in Hebrew is:

teaching.h: Words that connect ideas smoothly
teaching.p: Same core function as in every other language in this course — signaling how one idea relates to the next.
teaching.exTranslation: but, therefore, in addition, for example

teaching.h: אבל — everyday contrast
teaching.p: The most common, casual way to say 'but'.
teaching.ex: היא הייתה עייפה, אבל היא המשיכה לעבוד
teaching.exTranslation: hi haytah ayefah, aval hi himshikhah la'avod — She was tired, but she kept working

teaching.h: לכן — cause and result
teaching.ex: ירד גשם חזק, לכן ביטלו את המשחק
teaching.exTranslation: yarad geshem chazak, lakhen bitlu et ha-mischak — It rained heavily, therefore they cancelled the game

teaching.h: בנוסף — adding a point
teaching.ex: היא חכמה. בנוסף, היא חרוצה מאוד
teaching.exTranslation: hi chakhamah. be-nosaf, hi charutzah me'od — She's smart. In addition, she's very hardworking

quiz.q: ירד גשם חזק, ___ ביטלו את המשחק (therefore)
